name: Arna Jharna: The Thar Desert Museum of Rajasthan
notes:
The museum of brooms (etc.). I spent an eventful week here during the early stages of its construction—an ethnographic museum devoted to folk culture and the deep interconnection between ecology and daily life in Rajasthani communities. Ethnomusicology also played a central role, capturing the sounds and stories of the region. I was continually struck by how tightly environment and culture were woven, down to the specific materials used to make brooms—and the types of floors they were crafted to sweep.

Tragically, my time there was cut short by the unexpected death of one of the caretakers, a young man likely bitten by a venomous animal.

name: Mehrangarh Fort & the City of Jodhpur
notes:
As seen in The Dark Knight Rises. Blink and you'll miss it.

The blue city. I spent a brief period here with Rupayan Sansthan, a nonprofit focused on the ethnographic study of Rajasthan’s intangible cultural heritage. Founded by a folklorist who documented countless folk tales and musical traditions, the organization revealed fascinating links between culture, agriculture, and daily life. For example, dividing Rajasthan into three major agricultural zones—pearl millet, sorghum, and maize—correlates with differences in construction materials, diets, land use (pastoralism vs. agriculture), and even the types of musical instruments or household items like brooms that are traditionally made in each region. They built a museum out in the desert near Jodhpur.

Mehrangarh Fort has nothing to do with Rupayan Sansthan. It's just a really cool fort dominating the Jodhpur landscape, "a palace that might have been built by Titans and colored by the morning sun," according to Rudyard Kipling.

name: Pushkar
notes:
A sacred and spiritual town, often said to be home to the only temple dedicated to Brahma in India—though that’s not strictly true. It is, however, one of the very few temples honoring the Hindu god of creation. Devotees tend to favor Shiva and Vishnu, respectively the gods of destruction and protection, which I find a fascinating spiritual example of loss aversion—people are more motivated to ward off loss or protect what they have than to celebrate creation itself. Hundreds of temples surround the town’s holy lake, which is lined with ghats for ritual bathing. In short, this is a place steeped in mysticism and devotion—drawing both pilgrims in search of enlightenment and, inevitably, a fair share of hippies and mystics of more questionable credibility (read: quacks).

Every fall, during pilgrimage season, the town erupts into the famous Pushkar Camel Fair—a lively convergence of livestock trading, handicraft markets, and cultural spectacles. Ever wanted to race a camel or win the longest moustache contest? Here’s your chance.

name: Karni Mata Temple
notes: Yes, holy rats. The rare white ones are extra holy. Welcome to India.

name: Bikaner
description: Literally an oasis in the desert
notes:
Bikaner was once a key trading post along the caravan routes of the Thar Desert, and today it remains an oasis of culture—and camels—in the sand. Another former Rajput stronghold, it carries the architectural and martial legacy of princely India.

I visited with fellow students, ostensibly to see the infamous Karni Mata Temple, home to thousands of sacred rats. We balanced out the Rat Temple with a trip to Junagarh Fort, a striking example of medieval desert architecture, and made a stop at the National Research Centre on Camels, where camel husbandry is actively promoted—including through the commercial sale of camel milk products like lassi and ice cream. Naturally, that meant sampling some. Honestly? Not bad.

Right after we arrived, the sky opened up and dumped buckets of rain. In a city not built to handle stormwater, that meant we got flooded in for a day. Our hosts deemed our arrival auspicious—rain in the desert always is.

We were making it rain.

It was wild to see such a bone-dry place suddenly awash in water it didn’t know what to do with. Rumor had it that the World Bank was set to fund improved drainage systems the following year. True or not, the moment captured something bigger: how places shaped by scarcity must still grapple with sudden abundance, and how resilience takes many forms.

name: Alwar
description: "I have no memory of this place."
notes: Alwar, another former Rajput princely state, sits nestled in the ancient Aravalli Hills—among the oldest geological formations on Earth. Like many Rajasthani cities, it’s crowned by a hilltop fort, Bala Quila, predating the Mughal era and offering commanding views of the region. As a regional capital, Alwar benefits from its location in one of Rajasthan’s greener pockets, where the Aravalli range marks a natural transition, dividing watersheds, tempering the spread of the Thar Desert, and creating conditions more hospitable to humans in the eastern part of the state.
